title: A restless young man (1915)
hook: born in France, orphaned young, drifting through Cambridge and Columbia

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mystical Doctor: John of the Cross, a guide for the dark. Your line was the night is a way. Today, a new guide, and a very different life.

Rome, 1933. An eighteen-year-old wanders the city on his own. Both his parents are dead. He has money from a guardian, a head full of novels, and no plan. He goes into the old churches, not to pray, but to look at the mosaics, because he likes art. Standing in front of those gold and blue walls, something catches in him that he can't name. He'll spend years running from it. His name is Thomas Merton. He'll become the most famous monk in America, and for the next eighteen days he's the guide. Today: a restless young man.
screen: `ROME, 1933. EIGHTEEN, AND ALONE.` → `INTO THE CHURCHES FOR THE ART.` → `A RESTLESS YOUNG MAN.`

segments.voice: First, the losses. Merton was born on January 31, 1915, in Prades, a small town in the south of France. His father was a painter from New Zealand, his mother an American artist. When he was six, his mother died of cancer. When he was fifteen, his father died too. Then he was moved around: schools in France and England, holidays with relatives, a guardian in London. A boy with a suitcase, never quite at home. Second, the drifting. At Cambridge he drank, stayed out, failed at being careful, and left after a year he later looked back on with real shame. His guardian sent him to America. At Columbia University in New York he was clever, funny, restless. He wrote for the humor magazine, loved jazz, and flirted with politics. Busy all the time, happy almost never. Third, the mosaics. In those Roman churches he'd looked at pictures of Christ, and for the first time he wanted to know who that was. He didn't act on it yet. He just couldn't forget it. Fourth, why restless is a start. Long before Merton, Augustine wrote at the opening of his Confessions that the human heart is restless until it rests in God. Catholics have loved that sentence for sixteen hundred years. It doesn't treat restlessness as a failure. It treats it as a sign you're made for something you haven't found yet. Merton's early life looks like a mess. Read with Augustine, it looks like a search.
screen: `BORN IN FRANCE, ORPHANED YOUNG.` · `DRIFTING: CAMBRIDGE, THEN COLUMBIA.` · `THE MOSAICS HE COULDN'T FORGET.` · `RESTLESS UNTIL IT RESTS IN GOD.` · then, large: `A SEARCH, NOT A MESS.`

segments.voice: Get still, and notice what doesn't want to be still: the itch to check your phone, a thought that keeps circling, a sense that something's missing. Don't fix it or scold it; find where it lives in your body, your chest, your hands, your jaw, and gently ask it what it's looking for, without needing an answer. If you pray, you can offer the restlessness itself.
Inquietum. Augustine's Latin word for restless, used here for Thomas Merton at eighteen: orphaned, gifted, drifting, and carrying one picture from Rome he couldn't shake. Today's word.
Your line: restless is a start. The itch for something more can count as a beginning. Day two hundred seventy-two.

screen: `DAY 272 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A CONVERT IN NEW YORK (1938).`

howItsDone: Many Catholics read Thomas Merton's autobiography as a modern story of conversion, and Augustine's line about the restless heart is often quoted in Catholic preaching and in the Catechism itself.

fork.setup: you're eighteen, alone in Rome, and something in a church mosaic moves you. what do you do?
options: notice it, then go on drifting for years
fork.reveal: Merton didn't act on it for years. he went on drifting through Cambridge and Columbia, but he never forgot it.

original.note: Latin: restless, the word Augustine uses for the heart in the opening of his Confessions.

trapdoor: what you thought: Merton was a born monk.
what it means: he was an orphaned, gifted, drifting young man, and his restlessness was the start of the road.
what a scholar hears: Augustine's inquietum est cor nostrum, the restless heart, which Merton's readers heard echoed in his whole life story.
recall: the comfort God gives beginners in prayer
